ground_truth.title: The best fantasy, horror, and sci-fi books of 2025
ground_truth.author: Z.B. Steele
ground_truth.main_content:
It’s that time of the year for us to gather around a fire and talk about our favorite books of the year! Pour an egg-nog, grab the cookies, and get a towel as we go through the best fantasy, horror, and sci-fi books of 2025 as picked by the team here at Grimdark Magazine.

Strength of the Few by James Islington

Picked by Z.B.

Wildly ambitious and with so many jaw-dropping scenes and wonderful thematic work, Islington’s The Strength of the Few is my book of the year for 2025. Leading off from the incredible The Will of the Many, Vis’ adventure triples in complexity and scope, and Islington is leading all the threads on a triumphant and bold journey.

While the main strength of this novel is in its plot, the philosophical debates and powerful statements are more than welcome additions. Deep thoughts are beautifully stated, and this book promises to be the book 2 of an all time series.

Read our full review here.

About The Strength of the Few

OMNE TRIUM PERFECTUM

The Hierarchy still call me Vis Telimus. Still hail me as Catenicus. They still, as one, believe they know who I am.

But with all that has happened—with what I fear is coming—I am not sure it matters anymore.

I am no longer one. I won the Iudicium, and lost everything—and now, impossibly, the ancient device beyond the Labyrinth has replicated me across three separate worlds. A different version of myself in each of Obiteum, Luceum, and Res. Three different bodies, three different lives. I have to hide; fight; play politics. I have to train; trust; lie. I have to kill; heal; prove myself again, and again, and again.

I am loved, and hated, and entirely alone.

Above all, though, I need to find answers before it’s too late. To understand the nature of what has happened to me, and why.

I need to find a way to stop the coming Cataclysm, because if all I have learned is true, I may be the only one who can.

Read The Strength of the Few

Grave Empire by Richard Swan

Picked by Matt

This epic return to the Empire of the World setting, set 200 years later, brings us to a time of turmoil and upheaval. The ambassador to merfolk must face these terrifying creatures to seek their help against an even more ominous threat from the afterlife. Given they are no friend to her empire, and in some ways seem more like Lovecraftian horrors than Little Mermaid types, the ambassador has her work cut out for her. The story also follows a soldier sent to a jungle outpost to guard the empire’s outer colony against a rival empire, in what felt like an epic, horror version of the European conquest of the New World.

Read our full review here.

About Grave Empire

Blood once turned the wheels of empire. Now it is money.

A new age of exploration and innovation has dawned, and the Empire of the Wolf stands to take its place as the foremost power in the known world. Glory and riches await.

But dark days are coming. A mysterious plague has broken out in the pagan kingdoms to the north, while in the south, the Empire’s proxy war in the lands of the wolfmen is weeks away from total collapse.

Worse still is the message brought to the Empress by two heretic monks, who claim to have lost contact with the spirits of the afterlife. The monks believe this is the start of an ancient prophecy heralding the end of days—the Great Silence.

It falls to Renata Rainer, a low-ranking ambassador to an enigmatic and vicious race of mermen, to seek answers from those who still practice the arcane arts. But with the road south beset by war and the Empire on the brink of supernatural catastrophe, soon there may not be a world left to save…

Read Grave Empire

The Book that Held her Heart by Mark Lawrence

Picked by John

Mark Lawrence’s The Book That Held Her Heart, the final volume of his mind-bending Library Trilogy that began with The Book That Wouldn’t Burn and continued with The Book That Broke the World, delivers an emotional devastation that lingers long after the last page is turned. Written with Lawrence’s signature wit and gusto, the trilogy culminates in an ending so powerful it practically warrants a packet of tissues tucked between the final page and the back cover. As the perfect conclusion to Lawrence’s most ambitious work to date, The Book That Held Her Heart cements The Library Trilogy as one of the most profound and wholly original works of fiction I have encountered in the past two decades, an achievement that should place Mark Lawrence’s name in the same breath as other twenty-first-century masters of speculative fiction.

Read our full review here.

About The Book That Held Her Heart

Two people once connected by a vast and mysterious library are now separated and must overcome time and distance to reunite and bring peace to their worlds, in the final book of the Library Trilogy.

The fate of an infinite library hangs on one book, a book that holds the power to break the unbreakable. In the face of such forces, fragile things like hearts, worlds, and even family seem certain to fail.

The people most vital to Livira are scattered across time and space—lost, divided into factions, in mortal peril. Somehow she must bring them together and resolve the unresolvable argument that fuels the library’s war.

The bond between Livira and Evar has stretched and stretched again. Can it hold at the end, when things fall apart? Can it unite them against impossible odds?

This is the last chapter, the final page. The end threatens and no one—not characters, readers, or even the author—will emerge unscathed.

Read The Book That Held Her Heart

Obsidian Awakening by Sienna Frost

Picked by P.L.

There is no beginning. There is no end. There is only Obsidian – Revelation, Book Two of the Obsidian Series. This is the Alpha and the Omega for me, of the best of what Indie grimdark SFF is all about. Beyond audacious, soul crushingly dark, yet so elegantly beautiful it hurts to breathe, with some of the best prose I’ve ever read, that does not ask for compliance, it just takes you, and doesn’t give you back.

A part of my soul remained behind in this book, when I finished reading it.

My favorite author, the iconic Janny Wurts, read this book, praised it highly, and one quote from her Goodreads review of the novel sums up how incredible it is, far better than anything I ever could say: “Don’t plan on taking breaks, and don’t cry for mercy – this book will give you none.” Stop reading my review here, and just go buy both Book One Awakening, this book Revelation, and pray you have the strength to wait long enough for the next book in the series to be released.

Read our full review here.

About Obsidian Awakening

“You will live, with me, in the Black Tower, as my prisoner, my Bharavi, my wife. You will bear me a son, and he’ll grow, as a Rashai who will return to raid your land.”

He slaughtered her entire family.
He holds eight thousand prisoners hostage to keep her alive.
She lives every breath to see him die.
She remains the only thing in life he fails to conquer…and wants to.

Should one of them succeed, it will change the outcome of a centuries-long war between a nomadic race and an empire.

But they’re not the only ones holding the flint to light up the peninsula.

A teenage girl who can’t fight will wage war against an empire. A slave will rise to become her deadliest weapon. An oracle will lead them to impossible missions. A powerless prince will shift all alliances. A mysterious mastermind will make sure everyone dances to his tune.

Can they bring peace to the desert, or will they burn it all down?

Dive into an unforgettable world of endless sky, majestic dunes, desert warriors, powerful oracles, and deadly assassins, where love, loyalty, and honor burns in its scorching sand and the hearts of humans who refuse to run from a fight they can’t win.

Read Obsidian Awakening

Empire of the Dawn by Jay Kristoff

Picked by Aaron

A perfect conclusion to a stunning trilogy by a master storyteller. The bar was set high with Empire of the Vampire and Empire of the Damned but Empire of the Dawn might actually be the pick of the bunch. The twists and turns were non-stop and you are never really sure of who is going to make it out alive (or undead). This is a modern classic and such a brilliant way to end one of the best trilogies I have read. Vampires, sex, violence, grief, and an endless stream of twists and turns in a dark world praying for some light. Fuck my face indeed.

Read our full review here.

About Empire of the Dawn

From holy cup comes holy light;
The faithful hand sets world aright.
And in the Seven Martyrs’ sight,
Mere man shall end this endless night.

Gabriel de León has lost his family, his faith, and his last hope of ending the endless night—the Holy Grail, Dior. With no desire left but vengeance, he and a band of loyal brothers journey into the war-torn heart of the Augustin Empire to claim the life of the Forever King.

Unbeknownst to the Last Silversaint, the Grail still lives—speeding towards Augustin’s besieged capital in the frail hope of ending Daysdeath forever. But deadly treachery awaits within the halls of power, and the Forever King’s legions march ever closer. Gabriel and Dior will be drawn into a final battle that will shape the very fate of the Empire, but as the sun sets for what may be the last time, there will be no-one left for them to trust.

Read Empire of the Dawn

Tides of Torment by N.C. Scrimgeour

Picked by Esmay

Tides of Torment is without a shadow of a doubt my top pick of the year, because N.C. Scrimgeour absolutely obliterated my soul with this grand finale to the mythic and merciless Sea of Souls Saga, and I love her for that. The book hit immediately with a stunning “story so far” opening that had me crying before the real story had even started and then just never let up, charting a course through broken families, generational trauma, and the thin line between justice and ruin. I especially loved how Isla and Darce’s bond anchors the chaos with a raw vulnerability that cuts through the constant threat of selkies, sea serpents, pirates, deadly wraith mists, and other altogether more human horrors lurking in the deep. This is a finale that tears characters apart, rebuilds them in jagged pieces, and somehow still finds room for hope without ever softening its edges. It’s dark, gripping, and unforgettable, and it easily secures the Sea of Souls Saga as one of the most powerful fantasy series I have read in years.

Read our full review here.

About Tides of Torment

You told me you would haunt me, caraid. You were right.

The capital has fallen. Ghostly wraiths and bloodthirsty selkies roam the coast as the haar spreads its sickness across Silveckan. Every day, another port is consumed by the mist, and without her pelt, Isla Blackwood can do nothing to stop it.

Her only hope is to track down Eimhir, but her old friend has her own demons to battle, and she’s made it clear she doesn’t want to be found.

Instead, Isla must turn to the Sea Kith for an alliance. Their common enemy, the Grand Admiral, draws ever closer, and he won’t rest until the sea and everything in it is in his grasp once more.

Reunited with Darce and the soul bond they share, Isla prepares to sail into one last storm. If she survives it, she might be able to end decades of bloodshed between human and selkie. But if she fails, Silveckan will be lost to the mists forever…

Read Tides of Torment

Cthulhu: Grimoire by Eric Malikyte

Picked by CT

My favorite book this year has got to be Cthulu Grimoire by Eric Malikyte. A fantastic neo noir thriller with a Cthulhu bent. It is technically a sequel to Mind’s Horizon, a post-apocalypse novel, but works perfectly as a standalone (and is set in present-day Los Angeles anyway). How does that work? Well, you’d have to read the book to find out.

I really enjoyed this horror novel that manages to capture most of what I love about the Cthulhu Mythos with its madness, corruption, and alien nature but combined with the seediness of a gritty crime thriller. Mass suicides and strange religious cults mix well with a detective who has decided to make it his mission to protect an innocent being railroaded. Except, is the man actually innocent? There’s a lot of darkness here and some not-so-subtle social commentary that enhances rather than detracts from the horror.

Read our full review here.

About Cthulhu: Grimoire

Rejoice, for the Earth is His.

Detective Hunter will do anything to prove Dean Tyler’s innocence. The question is, is he willing to sacrifice his family to Cthulhu to do it?

All it takes is a single glance at a screen for the voices to take control. For idle hands to make things the human mind wasn’t meant to see. And for it to spread like wildfire.

Will he succumb to the virus plaguing the San Bernardino Valley and beyond?

Or can he find the will to stop it?

Read Cthulhu: Grimoire

Of Empires and Dust by Ryan Cahill

Picked by Rai

It’s not easy picking favourites, especially if you don’t want to sound like a broken record, but sometimes, your favourite book of the year comes early on and nothing seems to topple it. That’s the case for me this year with Of Empires and Dust from Ryan Cahill, the fourth novel in ‘The Bound and the Broken’ series. I know I picked it as my halfway point fave and, don’t get me wrong, a couple of books have come close to defeating it but just not quite (honorable mentions to The Devils and The October Film Haunt ).

How has it managed to stay at the top of my list for 2025 releases? I’m sure being the fourth novel, and seventh book, in this super expansive world with truly brilliant characters helps a lot. I’m invested. I’ve never read a series this long, and I am absorbed. The epic scale, the tragedies, the glimmers of humour, the frail humanity and, of course, the dragons were all on point in Of Empires and Dust. I don’t know how Ryan Cahill is going to top it, but I’m confident he will.

Read our full review here.

About Of Empires and Dust

I’ldryr viel asatar. I sanvîr viel baralun.

In fire we are forged. In blood we are tempered.

In the Aravell woodland, Calen Bryer grapples with the fallout from the Battle of Aravell. The path forward is littered with choices that will bleed him dry. But he is a Draleid, he is a guardian, and he will always stand when others call. He will be the light they look to.

His sister, Ella, lies fragmented, her mind split between worlds, her fate unknown. But the blood of the wolf is strong.

Hundreds of miles away, in the western villages of Illyanara, Dahlen Virandr leads the defense of Salme and all its inhabitants gathered from across the region. The Uraks are unrelenting, and they know only blood and death. If this is to be his end, he will enter Achyron’s Halls as a warrior who would not yield.

Below the mountains of Lodhar, Queen Kira waits in the dark while Hoffnar attempts to seize control of the Freehold and lead the dwarves towards a new dawn of war.

In Valtara, Dayne Ateres hunts those who betrayed his family, while Alina prepares her army to besiege the legendary Achyron’s Keep.

At the edges of the Burnt Lands, Rist Havel is offered a new path forward, one that few have ever trodden, one that could forge him into a mage of no equal.

With the news that Ilkya and Jormun have fallen, along with their soulkin, Eltoar finds himself face-to-face with Salara Ithan – a remnant of his past life that he had long thought dead.

As the Blood Moon taints the sky, Kallinvar and the Knights of Achyron battle tirelessly against the Shadow, doing everything within their power to hold back the darkness.

Gods are waking.
The world is burning.
Ashes and dust are all that will remain.

Read Of Empires and Dust

Hemlock & Silver by T. Kingfisher

Picked by Fiona

I quite like when the GdM puts together their best of lists. If my TBR hasn’t already been heavily influenced by this crowd, creating this always adds a few new reads to the tower. My personal favourite 2025 release was T. Kingfisher’s Hemlock & Silver, a bookish charcuterie board of dark fairytale fantasy, with a little bit of horror, and a smidgen of cosy stuff. Kingfisher is an author I will usually really enjoy, so I’m not surprised that Hemlock & Silver stands out to me. It springboards off the story of Snow White and has been spun into a Kingfisher original. I love the main character, Anja, she was witty, clever, darkly funny, and also just really wanted to be done having to fix other people’s problems so she could get back to her study and work with her poisons. Also, there’s a sassy feline animal companion; what more could you want?

Read our full review here.

About Hemlock & Silver

Healer Anja regularly drinks poison.

Not to die, but to save— seeking cures for those everyone else has given up on.

But a summons from the King interrupts her quiet, herb-obsessed life. His daughter, Snow, is dying, and he hopes Anja’s unorthodox methods can save her.

Aided by a taciturn guard, a narcissistic cat, and a passion for the scientific method, Anja rushes to treat Snow, but nothing seems to work. That is, until she finds a secret world, hidden inside a magic mirror. This dark realm may hold the key to what is making Snow sick.

Or it might be the thing that kills them all.

Read Hemlock & Silver

The Devils by Joe Abercrombie

Picked by Lucy

Anything this author writes I will pick up and inhale. As my pick for best book of 2025, The Devils is a fantastic, true-to-form return for Abercrombie, with a familiar mix of fast-paced bloody action scenes, scathing humour, and wonderfully written rag-tag group of anti-heroes. Crucially, it’s a book that doesn’t take itself too seriously, which makes it a nice palette (grimdark) cleanser. Away from his First Law world, I also really enjoyed getting to explore this bustling new AU medieval fantasy Europe. A League of Extraordinary Gentlemen meets Suicide Squad vibe, The Devils is a romp of a book with situations so nail-biting and (sometimes) absurd that it had me both cringing and cackling for most of the chapters. I can’t wait to see more of what the trilogy has to offer.

Read our full review here.

About The Devils

Holy work sometimes requires unholy deeds.

Brother Diaz has been summoned to the Sacred City, where he is certain a commendation and grand holy assignment awaits him. But his new flock is made up of unrepentant murderers, practitioners of ghastly magic, and outright monsters. The mission he is tasked with will require bloody measures from them all in order to achieve its righteous ends.

Elves lurk at our borders and hunger for our flesh, while greedy princes care for nothing but their own ambitions and comfort. With a hellish journey before him, it’s a good thing Brother Diaz has the devils on his side.

Read The Devils

The Red Labyrinth by Ben Peek

Picked by Adrian

I have been in a novella mood this year, and Ben Peek’s The Red Labyrinth really hit the spot for me. One of the things I loved about it the most was that it’s one of those books that reads according to your mood. If you want to get deep into the the societal commentary, there’s stuff for you to really get your teeth into. If you just want a cracking fantasy story, then that is there in spades as well. And as you know, the shorter form of writing has a big emphasis on the gut punch ending, and I think The Red Labyrinth will land with grimdark fans.

Read our full review here.

About The Red Labyrinth

The Red Labyrinth is the story of the anarchist Zoja Rose.

Presented to the reader as a speech given by Zoja’s most infamous disciple, Illanana, The Red Labyrinth tells of the violent histories of the Red King and the Black Queen, the twisted maze they lived in, and the cruel, tattooed monks who oversaw their rule.

Written by the critically acclaimed author Ben Peek, this dark fantasy brings his stylistic resourcefulness to bear in a compelling vortex of a short novel that is at once an existential journey, a harrowing exploration of the abuse of power, and a violent call to arms.

Read The Red Labyrinth

To Touch A Silent Fury by R.A. Sandpiper

Picked by Ed

Increasingly these days it’s the books that plough their own genre furrow that I often the find the most interesting. Take To Touch a Silent Fury, for example, the first in the Bride of Eavenfold duology by indie author R.A. Sandpiper. It’s described as an epic romantic fantasy, which might raise eyebrows for its inclusion in the tome of dark imaginings you’re currently reading, but trust me, that’s like describing a Swiss army knife as a bottle opener. Yes, the love story is compellingly well written – ultra slow-burn, complex, nuanced, and emotional in all the best ways, this is what I want to read when I read romance. But it could also be described as a grimdark political fantasy, given the Machiavellian court goings on and occasional bursts of mass slaughter, and the frequently grim yet deeply beautiful world Sandpiper has crafted is a triumph of imagination.

What we can say for sure about this book—in which the only woman in a magical brotherhood must marry the victor of a tournament to unlock her true powers, while a dragon prince conspires to stop her, all taking place in five intriguing lands based around the five senses—is that it contains some of the most satisfying and whip smart dialogue in all of SFF, a world of brutal politicking and court intrigue that will keep you glued to the page like an adhesive addict, and amongst all the unexpected slaughter has some of the most compelling, genuine, heartfelt, emotional beats that I know will move me for decades when I return to them. Sandpiper is doing remarkable stuff here, and 2025 saw her make a real claim for greatness.

Read our full review here.

About To Touch A Silent Fury

She rides to claim her fate, he flies to burn it down.

As the only woman in the Moontouched Brotherhood, Tani studies on the haughty island of Eavenfold surrounded by men who see her as an ill omen at best. Her Fate Ceremony is only days away, offering five possible escapes from the storm-locked island, but each with their own consequences.

Lang, an insubordinate Crown Prince, holds the reins to one of the few true dragons left in the world. Sent to Eavenfold on a diplomatic mission by his warmongering father, he watches as the Brothers bestow a rare and unwanted Marriage Fate on Tani. Already her touch magic alarms him, but if she succeeds and marries the victor of the upcoming tournament, her power could topple empires.

They both arrive at the games. Her, to claim her Fate. Him, to destroy it by any means possible.

Read To Touch A Silent Fury

The Everlasting by Alix E Harrow

Picked by Krystle

The Everlasting by Alix E Harrow was the best book/best spiritual experience of 2025. What Harrow accomplished in those pages is a stunning triumph, destined to be a modern classic in SFF. The Everlasting managed to be a conversation with the genre as a whole, exploring the concept of heroism and what it really means to be a legend, the scars of PTSD and how it changes a person, how gender fits/doesn’t fit into the tales we love to tell within the genre, and the darkest side of love and how we can save each other from own our toxic spirals (and/or toxic time travel) so that we can strive to be better versions of ourselves. Harrow has well earned her place as a pillar of the current SFF landscape, and The Everlasting is going to stay with me for years.

Read our full review here.

About The Everlasting

Sir Una Everlasting was Dominion’s greatest hero: the orphaned girl who became a knight, who died for queen and country. Her legend lives on in songs and stories, in children’s books and recruiting posters—but her life as it truly happened has been forgotten.

Centuries later, Owen Mallory—failed soldier, struggling scholar—falls in love with the tale of Una Everlasting. Her story takes him to war, to the archives—and then into the past itself. Una and Owen are tangled together in time, bound to retell the same story over and over again, no matter what it costs.

But that story always ends the same way. If they want to rewrite Una’s legend—if they want to tell a different story–they’ll have to rewrite history itself.

Read The Everlasting

When they Burned the Butterfly by Wen-Yi Lee

Set in 1972, Wen-Yi Lee’s historical fantasy, When They Burned the Butterfly, takes us to the cradle of a Singapore ablaze. A newly independent nation just seven-years young, Wen-Yi Lee’s Singapore is a fascinating setting, its buildings a gradient of crumbling and modern, its languages a mix of English, Hokkien, and Malay, and its people a medley of cultures, product of many years of immigration and colonization.

It uses this setting not only as a ground for exploration of the fantastic—for the influences that built this new Singapore are vast, and so are the myths, conflicts and gods brought with them—but as an element to explore the protean nature of identity; how fraught, fluid, ephemeral but wondrous it can be.

It is fascinating to realize how this newly founded nation is but a grander reflection of the novel’s characters, particularly Adeline Siow, a rebellious and fiery high-school graduate who abruptly loses her mother to a fire and finds herself chasing a girl with a butterfly tattoo that might hold more answers than Adeline first expected to ask. Her mother was not the first woman, nor the last, taken by the violence of a city in deadly transformation.

Like Singapore, Adeline finds herself navigating blood and rubble, but also love, on a journey to build her own identity, her own people and her own place, to give it word and define it, however wild the result may be. In the all-girl gang of Red Butterfly, amidst a simmering war between the Chinese gangs that once ruled the city, she finds this sense of identity and home, as well as horrific truths, and the girls journey parallels that of their city in beautiful, bloody, haunting ways.

It was Wen-Yi Lee’s mastery of both character and setting, the way they meld into one another, this unity between self, place and history, this exploration of the communal pain through which a community must fight to be born, along with the horrific body-horror scenes, that seared When They Burned the Butterfly into my mind like a vivid picture I can’t stop thinking about, and made it my favorite book of 2025.

About When they Burned the Butterfly

A fierce, glamorous sapphic fantasy reimagining the secret societies of postcolonial Singapore, for fans of Jade City, Silvia Moreno-Garcia, and the feverish intensity of RF Kuang’s Poppy War trilogy. Singapore, 1972: Newly independent and grappling for power in a fast-modernising world. Here, gangsters in Chinese secret societies are the last conduits of their ancestors’ migrant gods, and the back alleys where they fight are the last place magic has not been assimilated and legislated away.

Loner schoolgirl Adeline Siow has never needed more company than the flames she can summon at her fingertips. But when her mother dies in a house fire with a butterfly seared onto her skin, Adeline hunts down a girl she saw in a back-alley bar fight – a girl with a butterfly tattoo – only to discover that she’s far from alone.

Ang Tian is a Red Butterfly: one of a gang of girls who came from nothing, sworn to a fire goddess and empowered to wreak vengeance on the men that abuse and underestimate them. Adeline’s mother led a double life as their elusive patron, Madam Butterfly. Now that she’s dead, Adeline’s bloodline is the sole thing sustaining their link with this goddess. Between her search for her mother’s killer and the gang’s succession crisis, Adeline becomes quickly entangled with the girls’ dangerous world, and even more so with the charismatic Tian.

But no home lasts long around here. Ambitious and paranoid neighbour gangs hunt at the edges of Butterfly territory, and bodies are turning up in the red light district suffused with a strange new magic. Adeline may have found her place, but with the streets changing by the day, it may take everything she is to keep it.

Read When they Burned the Butterfly
